extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for mathematical contests/olympiads and instructors studying advanced trigonometry problem-solving
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and methods for advanced trigonometry problems (identities, inequalities, geometry, polynomial/trigonometric roots) typical of contest and olympiad training. Emphasizes specific techniques and transformations used to prove equalities, inequalities, and structural properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong induction for recurrence-defined polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: When polynomials are defined by recurrences (e.g., T0=1, T1=x, T_{i+1}=2xT_i - T_{i-1}), apply strong induction to prove parity, monotonicity, or identity properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prove T_{2n+1} is odd and T_{2n} is even by strong induction on n; prove monotonicity T_{n+1}(x) > T_n(x) > 1 for x>1 by assuming it for all ≤k and using the recurrence to derive it for k+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit parity (even/odd) properties of functions/polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and use whether a function or polynomial is even or odd to restrict roots and symmetries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chebyshev polynomials T_n are even for even n and odd for odd n; this is used to confine roots of T_n−1 to [−1,1] and analyze multiplicities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove and use the Chebyshev identity T_n(cos θ)=cos(nθ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show T_n(cos θ)=cos(nθ) (often by induction and product-to-sum formulas) and use it to determine polynomial values and roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: derive Tk+1(cos θ)=2 cos θ cos kθ − cos[(k−1)θ] and use product-to-sum to obtain cos[(k+1)θ]; then deduce explicit roots cos(kπ/2n), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate roots of trigonometric polynomials via inverse cosine mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the one-to-one mapping y=cos x on an appropriate interval to count and list real roots of T_n and related polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: T_n has n distinct real roots cos(kπ/2n), k=1,3,...,2n−1; roots of P_n(x)=T_n(x)−1 are cos(kπ/n) for certain parity-based index sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use product-to-sum, sum-to-product, and double/triple-angle identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard trigonometric transform identities to simplify expressions, convert differences/sums of sines/cosines into products, or relate multiple-angle expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout: e.g., 2 cos θ cos kθ = cos[(k+1)θ]+cos[(k−1)θ], sin u sin v conversions, and double/triple-angle manipulations to derive algebraic equations for cos(π/7) and similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the trigonometric form of Ceva’s theorem for concurrency
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the trig Ceva relation (product of certain sine ratios equals 1) to show concurrency of cevians in a triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a triangle with specified angle conditions, compute a ratio of sines and deduce lines AG, BD, CE concur, implying perpendicularity or other geometric conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce special triangle points (Brocard point) and exploit their properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Use known special points and their defining equal-angle properties to bound or compare angles in triangle problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use the Brocard point P with equal oriented angles α = ∠PAB = ∠PBC = ∠PCA to deduce that an interior point S lies in at least one triangle PAB,PBC,PCA and thus one angle ≤ α, then bound α using csc^2 identities and inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate inverse-trig squared sums (csc^2) and apply Cauchy–Schwarz
rubrics_metrics.description: Use identities expressing csc^2 of a constructed angle in terms of triangle angles and apply Cauchy–Schwarz (or other inequalities) to produce bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: csc^2 α = csc^2 A + csc^2 B + csc^2 C; apply Cauchy–Schwarz to show csc^2 α ≥ 4, hence α ≤ 30° in the Brocard-based argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Jensen’s inequality to concave functions like ln(sin x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize concavity (e.g., ln(sin x) on (0,π/2)) to apply Jensen and obtain product or average bounds of sines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in angle-sum problems, take f(x)=ln(sin x) with f''(x)<0 to compare sin(A−x)sin(B−y)sin(C−z) with sin of averaged arguments and deduce upper bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound products of sines via product-to-sum and double-angle inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algebraic/trig manipulations (2 sin x sin(A−x)=...) and known bounds like cos ≤1 to bound products like sin x sin(A−x) ≤ sin^2(A/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in alternative approaches, transform (sin x sin y sin z)^2 into product of sin x sin(A−x) etc., then bound each factor by sin^2(A/2) to deduce overall inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use telescoping sums with cot/cot differences for summation problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Express terms like 1/(sin k sin(k+1)) as cot k − cot(k+1) to create telescoping series and evaluate finite trigonometric sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sum 1/(sin 47 sin 48)+... telescopes to cot 45 − cot 90 etc.; widely used to reduce many contest summations to endpoint evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complex numbers and de Moivre’s formula to evaluate trigonometric sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Form complex sums ∑ z^k with z=cos a + i sin a and manipulate geometric series algebraically to obtain closed forms for sine/cosine sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compute Sn=∑ sin(k a) or express z+2z^2+... and extract imaginary part; used both as primary method and as alternative to telescoping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate algebraic sequences into trigonometric iterations (doubling rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize sequences defined by xn+1 = 4xn(1−xn) or xn+1 = xn + sqrt(1+xn^2) as sin^2(2θ) or tan-type recurrences, allowing closed-form expressions via angle-doubling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: letting a1=sin^2 θ gives a_n = sin^2(2^{n−1}θ), used to count parameter values where a_N=0 (roots at 2^{n−1}θ multiple of π). Also write xn=tan α to convert additive recurrences to angle-halving recurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Viète’s theorem and polynomial factorization to relate trig-function algebraic relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate multiple-angle trig equalities into polynomial equations (in tan^2, cos, etc.), then apply Viète relations to extract symmetric sums/products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: derive polynomial whose roots are tan^2(a), tan^2(2a), tan^2(3a) and use Viète to compute sums like tan^2 a + tan^2 2a + tan^2 3a = 21 etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply rational-root tests / Gauss’s lemma to prove irrationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert trig algebraic relations to rational-coefficient polynomials and use rational-root theorem to exclude rational roots, proving numbers like cos(π/7) are irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: convert an identity to a cubic in 2 cos a and note only ±1 possible rational roots — neither work — so 2 cos a is irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rearrangement / Chebyshev inequality arguments in symmetric inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Order sequences and apply rearrangement/Chebyshev to get bounds for sums like ∑ a x cos A ≤ ... when sequences have opposite monotonicities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a≥b≥c and cos A ≤ cos B ≤ cos C, use rearrangement to show ax cos A + ... ≤ (ax+bx+cx)(cos A+cos B+cos C)/3, leading to desired inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit geometric area and coordinate interpretations to prove trig inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Map trigonometric expressions to areas or coordinates (points on unit circle) and compare areas/rectangles to derive inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: represent sin x(cos x − cos y) as area of a rectangle inside the first-quadrant unit-circle sector and sum disjoint rectangle areas to bound π/4, yielding the inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pigeonhole principle with interval partitioning and sine mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the domain of an inverse trig mapping into equal-length intervals and apply pigeonhole to force two values to lie close, then translate to an inequality on sines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: map numbers a=2 sin x etc. into three intervals of length π/6; among four numbers two must map into the same interval, giving |x−y|≤π/6 and the desired bound on |sin(x−y)|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Schur’s inequality for symmetric trig polynomial inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert trig inequality into an algebraic symmetric inequality in cotangents (or other substitutions) and apply Schur to obtain the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reduce cot^3 A + cot^3 B + cot^3 C + 6 cot A cot B cot C ≥ cot A + cot B + cot C to a homogeneous Schur inequality after substituting x=cot A, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use law of sines and product-to-sum to solve geometry-with-point-angle conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply law of sines and product-to-sum formulas to relate ratios of segment lengths or sines of small angles, enabling exact angle computations in geometric constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a triangle with interior point P and several small specified angles, set x=∠PCB and express product of sine ratios to deduce x numerically (e.g., x=20°) and conclude isoscelesness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive integer-sided triangle similarity via cotangent/semi-perimeter relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate cot(A/2)= (s−a)/r to algebraic relations among cotangents, manipulate given weighted sums of cot^2 to obtain rational ratios of s−a, s−b, s−c and thus integer side ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set u=cot(A/2)= (s−a)/r etc., translate given quadratic relation into a sum-of-squares decomposition yielding proportionalities u:v:w and then map back to integer side lengths (13:40:45).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform minimization problems via symmetric substitution and single-variable reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine trig functions into a single auxiliary variable (e.g., c = sin x + cos x) and reduce the multi-term expression to a rational function in c for optimization using AM–GM or calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: minimize f(x)=sin x+cos x+tan x+cot x+sec x+csc x by setting c=a+b and expressing P(c)=... then apply AM–GM to find exact minimizing c and resulting minimum value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use telescoping via cosine differences for paired sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Express 2 sin 2k° sin 1° = cos(2k−1)° − cos(2k+1)° and use pairing to collapse sums of weighted sine terms into endpoint cos terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: used to show average of 2 sin 2°,4 sin 4°,...,180 sin 180° equals cot 1° by telescoping and pairing contributions to get 90 cos 1°/sin 1°.
